title: Talfan Buttonwood's Soggy Surprise
markdown:
The Grand Whispering Pines Hotel sat deep in the Whispering Woods like a held breath. In a salon the sun treated as its favourite room, Talfan Buttonwood’s Tea Emporium shone as if polish were a kind of faith. It was not merely a tea shop. It was a mole’s proof that the smallest place could be the greatest, if you cared enough about teaspoons.

Talfan Buttonwood had a flair that would have made an opera singer check the wings. His whiskers, cleaned and fluffed, twitched with the weight of a thousand tiny decisions. His voice could curdle milk or settle a squirrel, depending on the hour. Today the hour was major. Madam Evangeline Pumble, the Hotel Inspector, was due for her yearly visit. Talfan had spent weeks ironing cloth mats until they could have stood on their own, lining biscuits like soldiers who had never heard of crumbs, and making every teacup brighter than a jewel. The tunnels under the shop remained a soggy, persistent headache he kept meaning to have a word with.

“Jun, my good fellow,” Talfan announced, buffing a flowered cup until the light got ideas. “Have you seen the silver polish? It must shine as if it has just been dug from a pirate’s chest. Madam Pumble’s eyes miss nothing. A dull spoon is a stain on my soul.”

Jun, a crow whose feathers held the sheen of a well-kept night, perched on a lampshade and cocked his head. “Caw. Talfan, the tunnels are quite wet. There’s a drip-drip-drip by the pantry, like a tap that has invited friends. You might want to look before it becomes a waterfall with opinions.” His dark eyes held a mischievous glint. He had seen these jitters before.

Talfan waved a paw. The cloth kept moving. “Dampness is a wrinkle, Jun. Easily smoothed. Manners are the foundation of everything. Imagine Madam Pumble meeting an unpolished spoon. The horror. The scandal. A black mark on Whispering Pines hospitality.” He shivered as if the thought itself needed a napkin.

Madam Pumble arrived with spectacles that made her presence sharper. She scanned the salon like a hawk who also kept notes: spotless tables, flowers behaving themselves, and a slight tremor in Talfan’s paws. He wore his best emerald waistcoat, the one that made him look like a mole invented for tea. He beamed and poured. The china was Royal Bone, delicate as old skill. The biscuits sat in a circle almost too pretty to eat. For a moment the room held its breath and agreed to be perfect.

Then came an unwelcome sound. A tiny plink. Another. A dark spot no bigger than a forgotten raindrop appeared on the plaster above the main salon. It grew. The plink became a drip, then a rush, then a downpour. The salon, so carefully arranged, began to consider a career as a pond.

Talfan’s grand sentences collapsed into gasps. “My carpets. My antique sofa. The soggy humiliation.”

Jun dropped from the lampshade, a streak of black. “I told you about the tunnels. Now is not the time for polish. Buckets. Sponges. A very large duck, if you have one handy for distraction. Or a net, in case Madam Pumble fancies a swim.” The last suggestion sounded suspiciously like amusement.

Penelope Pipkin sashayed in from the hotel down the lane, a fox in a lavender suit that practised polite disapproval. Her smile was honey with a needle in it. “Oh, Talfan, dear. What an interesting water feature. So modern. Madam Pumble, I trust your visit is going swimmingly? I couldn’t help but notice a slight dampness. Perhaps a strategically placed napkin? A kind word to ease the inconvenience?” Her eyes caught the puddle and looked pleased to have been introduced.

The water rose toward the antique cabinet that held Talfan’s most precious things. He wrung his paws. He had been so busy looking effortless that he had forgotten the drip that was not a metaphor. Cold water found his feet. The air smelled of wet plaster, stressed mole, and biscuits beginning to reconsider their crispness. The polishing cloth hung from his fingers like a flag that had surrendered too early.

“My reputation,” Talfan said, voice shaking, “ruined by a leaky pipe and too much politeness. Penelope, your helpful advice seems to involve standing there looking decorative while my salon becomes a swamp.”

A treasured cup — Royal Bone China, painted with tiny golden pheasants, a gift from a visiting Duchess — wobbled on the edge of a flooded table. It drifted toward a drain grate. Penelope tutted, a sound like a sigh that had dressed for company. “What a pity. One tries to be ready for anything. Sometimes things just happen. Such is the unpredictable nature of life.”

Jun’s caw cut the polite weather. “Enough. Polite problems are still problems. And that cup is heading for the plumbing abyss.” He swooped, not gently, and shoved the china with his beak. It skittered onto the slightly drier carpet. He landed in a flurry that sent a fresh wave onto Penelope’s lavender suit.

The messy rescue shook Talfan out of his panic. He looked at Jun, proud in the middle of the minor flood, then at Penelope, whose sweet smile had developed a leak of its own. Jun had acted. Talfan dropped the polishing cloth. It made a small, honest thud.

“Jun. Well done. Absolutely brilliant.” He turned to Penelope with a new firmness. “If you are not going to be helpful, perhaps you could fetch a really, really large towel. Or a very enthusiastic sponge. One that does not merely watch water, but argues with it.”

Madam Pumble watched. The sternness in her face softened until it wrinkled the corners of her eyes. Talfan felt relief that had nothing to do with silver.

“I have inspected hundreds of hotels,” she said, warm over the drip and the flap of feathers. “Many are perfect. Neat, efficient, and utterly forgettable. Few have characters like this. A mole who believes in manners even when his ceiling is crying. A crow who acts before he thinks. And others who offer very polite comments while the world gets messy.” She chuckled, a hearty sound. “The leak is being handled by my groundskeeper, whom I have discreetly asked to assist. The teacup is safe, and I have had more fun than I have had in months. Talfan, your establishment has spirit. That, my dear mole, is worth more than all the polished silver in the world.”

Talfan Buttonwood laughed then, a real rumble, the sort that belonged to earth. Penelope, surprised by genuine laughter, managed a small embarrassed smile. Jun preened on the table and offered a triumphant caw that meant, quite clearly, I did mention the pantry. In the salon, the sun still tried to make mosaics on the wet floor. The cloth stayed where it had fallen. The silver, for once, was allowed to wait.
characters: Talfan Buttonwood (dramatic mole tea shop owner), Jun (crow friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
